walkthroughs.body_html:
The Water Cycle & Water Insecurity — a core area of A-Level Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The Water Cycle & Water Insecurity brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The Water Cycle & Water Insecurity.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Where does the Keeling Curve come from?
options: Hawaii
Antarctica
California
Norway

mcqs.q: Methane is how many times more potent than CO2?
options: 2x
It is only water evaporating from puddles and lakes.
The combined loss of water from a surface through evaporation (from soil and water bodies) and transpiration (from plant leaves).
Humans affect the carbon cycle by eating plants.
It is the process of rain falling from clouds.

mcqs.q: Why are tropical rainforest soils typically infertile?
options: Because rainforest soils are made of clay.
Because so much vegetation grows there, the soil must be fertile.
It is the process of rain falling from clouds.
Heavy rainfall leaches nutrients, and most nutrients are stored in living biomass and rapidly recycled — the soil itself holds very little.

mcqs.q: How do humans affect the carbon cycle?
options: Humans affect the carbon cycle by eating plants.
By burning fossil fuels (releasing stored geological carbon to the atmosphere) and deforestation (reducing the biosphere store and releasing carbon).
Humans only affect the carbon cycle by breathing out CO2.
It is the process of rain falling from clouds.
